title: The Mean Value Theorem
lead: If a smooth function takes equal values at the ends of an interval, its graph has a horizontal tangent in between. This section states that fact, Rolle’s theorem, and its slanted form, the Mean Value Theorem, and draws three consequences used for the rest of the chapter.
objectives: Explain the meaning of Rolle’s theorem.
Describe the significance of the Mean Value Theorem.
State three important consequences of the Mean Value Theorem.
summary_html:
• If $\kf$ is continuous over $[a,b]$ and differentiable over $(a,b)$ and $\kf(a)=\kf(b),$ then there exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that $\kfprime(c)=0.$ This is Rolle’s theorem.
  • If $\kf$ is continuous over $[a,b]$ and differentiable over $(a,b),$ then there exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that
$$\kfprime(c)=\frac{f(b)-\kf(a)}{b-a}.$$

This is the Mean Value Theorem.

  • If $\kfprime(x)=0$ over an interval $\kI,$ then $\kf$ is constant over $\kI.$
  • If two differentiable functions $\kf$ and $\kg$ satisfy $\kfprime(x)=\kgprime(x)$ over $\kI,$ then $\kf(x)=\kg(x)+C$ for some constant $C.$
  • If $\kfprime(x)\gt 0$ over an interval $\kI,$ then $\kf$ is increasing over $\kI.$ If $\kfprime(x)\lt 0$ over $\kI,$ then $\kf$ is decreasing over $\kI.$

exercises.prompt: Why do you need continuity to apply the Mean Value Theorem? Construct a counterexample.

answer.solution: Without continuity over $[a,b]$ the graph may jump, and the secant’s slope need not be the slope of any tangent. For example, let $f(x)=x$ for $0\le x\lt 1$ and $f(1)=0.$ Then $f$ is differentiable over $(0,1),$ with $f'(x)=1$ there, but $\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0,$ and no $c\in(0,1)$ has $f'(c)=0.$ The theorem fails because $f$ is not continuous at the endpoint $x=1.$

exercises.prompt: Why do you need differentiability to apply the Mean Value Theorem? Find a counterexample.
When are Rolle’s theorem and the Mean Value Theorem equivalent?

answer.solution: They are equivalent when $f(a)=f(b):$ then the secant line joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$ is horizontal, its slope $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ is $0,$ and the Mean Value Theorem’s conclusion $f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ becomes Rolle’s conclusion $f'(c)=0.$ Conversely, the Mean Value Theorem is proved from Rolle’s theorem applied to $g(x),$ the vertical difference between $f$ and the secant line.

exercises.prompt: If you have a function with a discontinuity, is it still possible to have ${f}^{'}(c)(b-a)=f(b)-f(a)?$ Draw such an example or prove why not.

answer.solution: Yes, but the Mean Value Theorem still does not apply

answer.solution: Here $f(1)-f(-1)=1-1=0,$ so we would need $f'(c)(2)=0,$ that is, $f'(c)=0.$ But $f'(x)=-\frac{2}{x^{3}}$ is never $0,$ so there is no such $c.$ The Mean Value Theorem does not apply because $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ is not defined at $x=0,$ so it is not continuous over $[-1,1].$

$f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor$ (Hint: This is called the floor function and it is defined so that $f(x)$ is the largest integer less than or equal to $x.)$

answer.solution: Here $f(1)-f(-1)=1-(-1)=2,$ so we would need $f'(c)(2)=2,$ that is, $f'(c)=1.$ But the floor function is constant between consecutive integers, so wherever it is differentiable $f'(x)=0;$ there is no such $c.$ The Mean Value Theorem does not apply because $\lfloor x\rfloor$ jumps at $x=0$ (and at $x=1$), so it is not continuous over $[-1,1].$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, consider the roots of the equation.

Show that the equation $y={x}^{3}+4x+16$ has exactly one real root. What is it?

answer.solution: Let $f(x)=x^{3}+4x+16.$ Since $f(-2)=-8-8+16=0,$ $x=-2$ is a root. Since $f'(x)=3x^{2}+4\gt 0$ for all $x,$ $f$ is increasing over $(-\infty,\infty)$ by Corollary 3, so it takes the value $0$ only once. (If it had two roots $a\lt b,$ Rolle’s theorem would give $c$ with $f'(c)=0.$) The equation has exactly one real root, $x=-2.$

For the following exercises, consider the roots of the equation.

Find the conditions for $y={e}^{x}-b$ to have one root. Is it possible to have more than one root?

answer.solution: Since $e^{x}\gt 0$ for all $x,$ the equation $e^{x}-b=0$ has a root only when $b\gt 0,$ and then the root is $x=\ln b.$ It cannot have more than one root: $y'=e^{x}\gt 0,$ so $y=e^{x}-b$ is increasing over $(-\infty,\infty)$ by Corollary 3, and an increasing function takes the value $0$ at most once.

At 10:17 a.m., you pass a police car at 55 mph that is stopped on the freeway. You pass a second police car at 55 mph at 10:53 a.m., which is located 39 mi from the first police car. If the speed limit is 60 mph, can the police cite you for speeding?

answer.solution: Yes. You drove $39$ mi between 10:17 a.m. and 10:53 a.m., in $36$ min $=0.6$ h, so your average speed was $\frac{39}{0.6}=65$ mph. Your position is a differentiable function of time, so by the Mean Value Theorem there was a moment in that time when your velocity equaled the average velocity, $65$ mph, which is over the speed limit of $60$ mph.

Two cars drive from one stoplight to the next, leaving at the same time and arriving at the same time. Is there ever a time when they are going the same speed? Prove or disprove.

answer.solution:
Yes

Let ${s}_{1}(t)$ represent the distance of Car 1 from Stoplight 1 at time $t$. Let ${s}_{2}(t)$ represent the distance of Car 2 from Stoplight 1 at time $t$. Then ${s}_{1}(0)=0={s}_{2}(0)$. Let $t=m$ represent the time that the cars arrive at Stoplight 2. Then ${s}_{1}(m)=d={s}_{2}(m)$ where $d$ is the distance between the stoplights.

Define a new function $f(t)={s}_{1}(t)-{s}_{2}(t)$. Then $f(0)=0=f(m)$. By the Mean Value Theorem, there is a time $0\lt c\lt m$ such that

${f}^{'}(c)=\frac{f(m)-f(0)}{m-0}=\frac{0}{m}=0.$

At time c,

${f}^{'}(c)=0$

${s}_{1}^{'}(c)-{s}_{2}^{'}(c)=0$

${s}_{1}^{'}(c)={s}_{2}^{'}(c)$

So, at time c, Car 1 and Car 2 are traveling at the same speed.

Show that $y={\sec}^{2}x$ and $y={\tan}^{2}x$ have the same derivative. What can you say about $y={\sec}^{2}x-{\tan}^{2}x?$

answer.solution: By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dx}\sec^{2}x=2\sec x(\sec x\tan x)=2\sec^{2}x\tan x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{2}x=2\tan x\sec^{2}x,$ the same derivative. By Corollary 2, $\sec^{2}x-\tan^{2}x$ is a constant over any interval on which both are defined; indeed $\sec^{2}x-\tan^{2}x=1,$ the Pythagorean identity.

Show that $y={\csc}^{2}x$ and $y={\cot}^{2}x$ have the same derivative. What can you say about $y={\csc}^{2}x-{\cot}^{2}x?$

answer.solution: By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dx}\csc^{2}x=2\csc x(-\csc x\cot x)=-2\csc^{2}x\cot x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\cot^{2}x=2\cot x(-\csc^{2}x)=-2\csc^{2}x\cot x,$ the same derivative. By Corollary 2, $\csc^{2}x-\cot^{2}x$ is a constant over any interval on which both are defined; indeed $\csc^{2}x-\cot^{2}x=1,$ the Pythagorean identity.<sup class="fn" data-note="c-key-193"></sup>
